title: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say 2,000-km missile range limit 'lifted'; tanker hits mine near Hormuz
dek: The IRGC spokesman says Iran will show its capabilities 'in practice' as US strikes on Qeshm continue and Qatar presses a two-day plan to reopen the strait.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards have said the country no longer considers itself bound by the 2,000-kilometre limit it had placed on the range of its ballistic missiles, a statement made as US and Iranian forces traded fire around the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf mediators tried to hold together a plan to end the confrontation.

"That restriction has been lifted for us," General Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), told a press conference in Tehran on Saturday, according to reports. He did not say whether Iran already has missiles that can fly further, saying only that Iran would "demonstrate these capabilities in practice" rather than make statements. Iran's military separately said that a tanker sailing east of the strait with its transponder switched off had hit a naval mine and caught fire.

## What happened

Mr Mohebbi's remarks came days after Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered what Iranian media described as an "unrestrained" military response to any future threat from the United States or Israel, and said retaliation would have no geographic limits, according to reports. Mr Mohebbi also said the IRGC would soon unveil another underground "missile city", one report said.

Iran is not known to have missiles with a range beyond 2,000 km, according to reports. A missile of that range can already reach the whole Arabian Peninsula, the Levant, most of Egypt and parts of Greece and the Balkans. US officials have said that technology from Iran's space launch programme could be repurposed to build intercontinental ballistic missiles, according to reports.

The statement followed two nights of US strikes. Iranian state media reported two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, at the mouth of the Gulf, late on Friday. President Donald Trump, speaking in West Palm Beach, Florida, on Friday evening, confirmed the strike and called it minor, saying Iran had "built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device" which US forces "knocked out" within minutes. US officials have described this week's strikes on Qeshm, Hengam and Bandar Abbas as defensive action against surface-to-air missile sites, not a return to full-scale combat, reports said.

Iran's army said early on Saturday that it had shot down a US MQ-9 Reaper drone with a new air-defence system it did not name. The IRGC said on Friday that it had intercepted an MQ-1 drone. The US has not confirmed either loss, and the claims could not be independently verified.

On the mine, Iran's military did not name the tanker or give its flag or destination. It said the ship was sailing in a "prohibited area". Washington has said that the mines Iran laid in the strait have been cleared, according to reports. There was no immediate word on casualties.

## The diplomacy

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that he had spoken to 12 foreign ministers in 48 hours, including those of Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, and had set out Iran's "fundamental positions", including seven conditions for reopening the strait, according to reports. He called for regional security arrangements "without the interference of superregional powers". He also spoke to Iraq's foreign minister, Fuad Hussein, on Friday.

Qatar is pushing a two-day "bridge" plan, according to reports citing unnamed officials. On the first day, the US would lift its blockade of Iranian ports and release some frozen Iranian assets, and Iran would let International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors into sites bombed by the US and Israel. On the second day, Iran would reopen Hormuz under a temporary arrangement with Oman. Wider nuclear talks would follow. The White House has declined to comment on the proposal. Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, has urged both sides not to wait for a "perfect moment". Mr Trump spoke to Qatar's emir by phone on Friday, and US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth spoke to his Qatari counterpart.

Iran's conditions, according to reports citing unnamed officials, are an end to the port blockade, the lifting of sanctions, the release of frozen assets, compensation for war damage, and an end to hostilities across the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon. A senior Iranian official said nuclear talks could begin only after those conditions were met, one report said.

## Background

The US and Israel have bombed Iranian nuclear and military sites, and Iran has restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel through which most Gulf oil and gas exports normally pass. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO), which monitors merchant shipping, said in its weekly report that at least 11 ships had been attacked in and around the strait in the week to 6 November and three had sunk, according to reports. It counted 170 outbound and 155 inbound transits, about 65% below pre-conflict levels. Many tankers now cross on a southern route near Oman with their transponders switched off.

The IAEA says Iran held 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60% as of 13 June 2025, and that it has been unable to verify the stockpile since the strikes.

Pressure on Washington has grown since Tuesday's US midterm elections, in which Republicans lost control of both houses of Congress. Voter anger over the war and high fuel prices contributed, according to reports. The new Congress sits in January. Mr Trump has since named Stephen Miller as his chief of staff.

## Why it matters for India

India imports most of its crude oil and liquefied natural gas from the Gulf, and much of it normally passes through Hormuz. Every week the strait stays restricted keeps freight and insurance costs high for Indian refiners and adds risk for the many Indian seafarers who crew tankers in the region. A wider missile range would also widen the area that could be drawn into any renewed war, including Gulf states where millions of Indians live and work. India has not commented on the IRGC statement.

## What happens next

Mediators are expected to keep working on the Qatari plan over the weekend. Washington has not said whether it accepts the proposed sequence, and Iran says it will not fully reopen the strait until its conditions are met. US Central Command has offered a reward of up to $20 million for information on Iran's nuclear programme.

## Key numbers

- 2,000 km: the missile range limit Iran says it has lifted
- 11: ships attacked in and around Hormuz in the week to 6 November, three of them sunk, according to UKMTO figures cited in reports
- 65%: fall in Hormuz transits from pre-conflict levels, by the same count
- 440.9 kg: Iran's 60% enriched uranium, last verified by the IAEA in June 2025
- 12: foreign ministers Mr Araghchi says he spoke to in 48 hours
